article_text:
Die Folgen der vorzeitigen Schließung der Art Basel Paris, Steuervorteile für Kunstschenkungen an Museen und ein Nachruf auf die Bildhauerin Ursula von Rydingsvard: Das ist unsere Medienschau am Dienstag

Kunstmarkt

Melanie Gerlis analysiert in der "Financial Times" die Folgen der vorzeitigen Schließung der Art Basel Paris und fragt, ob solche Abbrüche angesichts wachsender geopolitischer Spannungen künftig häufiger werden. Die Messe sei ein offensichtliches Protestziel gewesen: Was symbolisiere eine abgehobene Bourgeoisie besser als "ein kleines Glashaus voller teurer Kunst"? Sie verweist auf den Zusammenhang zwischen dem Wachstum des Kunstmarkts und globaler Vermögensungleichheit. Die Finanzwissenschaftlerin Rachel Pownall warnt, der Markt sei als Luxussegment besonders abhängig von wenigen sehr reichen Akteuren. Ein Galerist betont jedoch, dass "80 Prozent der Künstler und Galerien" ums wirtschaftliche Überleben kämpften und die gewaltfreien Proteste unterstützten. Pownall fragt, wann Ungleichheit und fehlende Chancengleichheit einen Kipppunkt erreichen, der weitere Aufstände auslösen könnte.

Olga Kronsteiner erläutert im "Standard" , wie steuerliche Anreize Kunstschenkungen an Museen fördern – besonders in den USA, wo private Spender den Marktwert geschenkter Werke unter bestimmten Bedingungen bis zu 30 Prozent ihres Bruttoeinkommens steuerlich geltend machen können. Prominente Beispiele sind die Übernahme der New Yorker Neuen Galerie durch das Metropolitan Museum samt mehr als 600 Kunstwerken und einem Fonds von 200 Millionen Dollar sowie eine Schenkung von 130 Werken an das LACMA, darunter Gemälde von Gustav Klimt und Egon Schiele. In Österreich sei die Absetzbarkeit deutlich begrenzter: Privatpersonen und Unternehmen könnten grundsätzlich zehn Prozent ihrer Einkünfte beziehungsweise Gewinne ansetzen. Dennoch profitieren die Bundesmuseen von umfangreichen Zuwendungen. Allein die Albertina habe 2025 Kunstwerke im Wert von rund vier Millionen Euro erhalten darunter Arbeiten von Sean Scully und Brigitte Kowanz. Welche steuerlichen Vorteile Schenkungen lebender Künstlerinnen und Künstler bringen, bleibe in Österreich allerdings Geschäftsgeheimnis, so Kronsteiner.

Skulptur

Will Heinrich würdigt in der "New York Times" die am heutigen Dienstag im Alter von 84 Jahren gestorbene Bildhauerin Ursula von Rydingsvard . Bekannt wurde sie für monumentale, aus zahlreichen Zedernholzbalken zusammengesetzte Skulpturen, deren organische Formen an Höhlenwände, gefrorene Wellen oder Muscheln erinnern. Die Arbeit der in Deutschland Geborenen verband die Wiederholung industrieller Bauteile mit sinnlichen, individuellen Formen und widersprach damit der als unmenschlich empfundenen Strenge des Minimalismus. Das Holz sei "wie Butter", sagte die Künstlerin einmal: Es gebe leicht nach, sei sinnlich und beinahe rosa. Ihre Skulpturen sollten auch im öffentlichen Raum zugänglich sein: "Ich würde es sogar toll finden, wenn Menschen sie berühren."

Hillary Clinton hat vor der Verleihung des Praemium Imperiale die japanische Insel Naoshima besucht und vor Kürbisskulpturen der kürzlich verstorbenen Künstlerin Yayoi Kusama posiert. Auf Instagram bezeichnete die frühere US-Außenministerin Kunst als Gegenmittel in schwierigen Zeiten: "In einer manchmal dunklen und chaotischen Welt ist Kunst ein Gegenmittel gegen Abstumpfung und mangelnde Neugier. Sie erinnert uns daran, dass schöpferisches Handeln ein Akt des Widerstands ist." Clinton ist seit 2022 internationale Beraterin des renommierten Kunstpreises und Vorsitzende des US-amerikanischen Nominierungskomitees. Bei der 37. Verleihung in Tokio werden fünf Persönlichkeiten ausgezeichnet , darunter die US-Künstlerin Jenny Holzer, der britische Bildhauer Andy Goldsworthy, der Architekt Daniel Libeskind, der schwedische Musiker Herbert Blomstedt und die australische Schauspielerin Cate Blanchett.

article_text:
Jenna Ortega hopes that her new film, the dystopian sci-fi “ Klara and the Sun ,” can remind people to live in the moment in the age of AI and all-consuming technology.

“I think we gotta put our focus on one another and put down the computers and phones,” the star told Variety on the red carpet at the movie’s world premiere at London Film Festival on Thursday night.

Ortega, wearing a stunning yellow lace dress and hair piece, added: “Remember to be present and to appreciate people while they’re standing right in front of you.”

Based on Nobel Prize winner Kazuo Ishiguro’s bestselling 2021 novel of the same name, “Klara and the Sun” is set in a future where advances in genetic engineering have divided humans into strict social classes. Ortega plays Klara, an artificial android companion who is purchased for an ailing girl named Josie (Mia Tharia). “Klara and the Sun” is directed by “Thor” helmer Taika Waititi and also stars Amy Adams as Josie’s mother, Aran Murphy (son of Cillian Murphy), Natasha Lyonne, Steve Buscemi and more.

Popular on Variety

Waititi, Adams, Murphy and Lyonne all walked the London Film Festival red carpet on Thursday night, alongside Waititi’s wife Rita Ora, author Ishiguro and a surprise appearance from Florence Pugh, who stunned in a blue floral gown with statement sleeves. Pugh enthusiastically greeted Ortega and Adams before they all posed for photos together alongside producer Rachel Forman.

Standing alongside Ortega, Adams added that everyone she’s spoken to has gotten “something different” out of the film. “That, to me, is a really successful film that communicates something different to each viewer. So I like hearing what people get out of it,” she said.

Ortega clarified that though Klara is an “artificial friend,” she doesn’t work like the AI that we know today.

“AI I guess pulls all this information from the internet and Klara gets all her information from the real world,” she said. “So that’s a little bit different. She’s kind of like a toddler in a sense. Playing her specifically in this film was really interesting because Taika wanted a more human approach, so he didn’t want to do movement that was too robotic, maybe more sort of clumsy and unknowing.”

Waititi echoed Ortega in saying that the film’s message is to “put the phone down.”

“I would just like people to remember what friendship is, connect with people and just be,” he said. “Just be in the moment.”

Ishiguro acknowledged that, since his novel came out in 2021, the world’s awareness and attitude about AI has changed greatly.

“This film doesn’t address a lot of the anxieties that you and I may have right now about where we’re going with the technology. I mean, I think quite rightly, it’s really come center stage,” he said. “I’m aware that this film is coming out into a very different world to the one that my novel came out in five years ago, and I don’t know how that will change people’s expectations or how people look at things. But I’ll say that this isn’t another film about how an AI machine seems to be nice and then becomes sinister and ends up killing all the nice people in the film. It’s not that sort of story.”

Ishiguro is wading more into film, confirming to Variety that he’s working on a new project with Tim Burton, for which he penned an original script. Though Burton and Ishiguro have a mutual friend in “Wednesday” star Ortega, he said she’s not the one who introduced them.

“I thought this was supposed to be a big secret!” Ishiguro said. “No, Jenna didn’t introduce us. Tim lives quite near where I live in North London, and I was dropping in on him in his very strange and wacky and beautiful house. I mean, it looks like a Tim Burton set. And we started to talk about a project and I wrote a script on spec. We decided to just do it privately between the two of us, and then take it to people.”

He added that it’s not a “war film,” saying: “Genre-wise, it’s very hard to pigeonhole. It’s a Tim Burton film!”

“Klara and the Sun” is set to hit theaters via Sony Pictures on Oct. 23.

article_text:
1600年前の「変色する聖杯」を現代科学で再現──「世界のガラス七不思議」の謎に迫る

大英博物館 が所蔵する4世紀の「リュクルゴスの聖杯」は、光の当たり方によって緑色にも赤色にも見える。イギリスのシェフィールド大学の研究チームは、金と銀のナノ粒子を利用し、古代ローマの職人が生み出した色の変化を再現することに成功した。

大英博物館 に所蔵されているリュクルゴスの聖杯は、通常は緑色に見えるが、背後から光を当てると赤色に変化する特性を持つ。この不思議な現象は長年研究者たちを悩ませてきたが、イギリスのシェフィールド大学の研究チームが、実物に近い色の変化を再現することに成功した。研究に携わったリサ・ホランズは、ガーディアン紙のインタビューで次のように 語っている 。

「私にとって、この研究は情熱を注いで取り組んできた仕事です。これまでにも再現を試みた人はいましたが、成果は限定的でした。私にはまるで魔法のように思えます」

4世紀に制作されたこの杯には、ホメロスの叙事詩『イリアス』第6巻に登場するリュクルゴス王の神話を題材とした浮き彫りが施されている。描かれているのは、ワインの神ディオニュソスに敗れ、ブドウのつるに絡め取られたリュクルゴス王の姿だ。また、この杯は2022年、国連が定めた「国際ガラス年」の関連事業で「世界のガラス七不思議」のひとつに選ばれている。

研究チームは、金と銀を加えたガラスを高温で溶かし、冷却する過程でナノサイズの結晶を形成することに成功した。ガーディアン紙によれば、これらの粒子の大きさは砂粒の約1000分の1だという。ホランズは、こうした微細な粒子によってガラスの色が変化する仕組みを次のように説明している。

「このガラスに光を透過させると、金と銀の粒子が青と緑の光を遮断し、赤とオレンジの光だけを通過させます。一方、ガラスの表面で光が反射する場合は、粒子が光を散乱させるため、私たちの目には不透明な緑色に見えるのです。もしローマ人たちが私の実験を見ていたら、どうしてこんなものの作り方も知らないんだ、って笑うでしょうね」

シェフィールド大学の依頼を受け、ガラス作家のエリオット・ウォーカーは、今回再現されたガラスを使った彫刻作品を制作した。この作品は、11月に同校が主催する「Festival of the Mind」の一環として、シェフィールド市内のミレニアム・ギャラリーで展示されたのち、大学内のターナー・ガラス美術館で常設展示される予定だ。

こうした色の変化には、装飾の他に意味があった可能性もある。ユニヴァーシティ・カレッジ・ロンドンの考古材料学名誉教授、イアン・フリーストーンは、緑から赤への変化がブドウの実の成熟を象徴しているのではないかと推測し、次のように語っている。

「描かれている場面は、ブドウのつるがリュクルゴスを冥界へと引きずり込んでいるところです。ですから、この杯は何らかの飲酒の儀式で使われていた可能性があります」

（翻訳：編集部）

article_text:
Im venezianischen Palazzo Grassi wird künftig die Sammlungspräsentation der Pinault Collection in einer Dauerausstellung zu sehen sein

Die Schau soll am 21. März 2027 eröffnet werden. Gezeigt werden mehr als 100 bedeutende Werke moderner und zeitgenössischer Kunst. Bislang beherbergte das Haus am Canal Grande Wechselausstellungen, seit der Eröffnung im Jahr 2006 insgesamt 27.

Die Pinault Collection umfasst nach eigenen Angaben mehr als 10.000 Werke moderner und zeitgenössischer Kunst. Zu ihr gehören die Privatmuseen Bourse de Commerce in Paris sowie der Palazzo Grassi und die Punta della Dogana in Venedig.

Ebenfalls am 21. März 2027 beginnt in der Punta della Dogana in Venedig die Ausstellung "Tadao Ando & Mono-ha. The Five Elements", die bis zum 21. November 2027 läuft. Sie widmet sich dem japanischen Architekten Tadao Ando, der alle drei Museen der Pinault Collection gestaltet hat, und stellt Fotografien seiner Architekturprojekte den Arbeiten der japanischen Mono-ha-Bewegung gegenüber.

In der Pariser Bourse de Commerce, die ebenfalls von der Pinault Collection bespielt wird, eröffnet am 3. März 2027 die Ausstellung "Infini". Rund 60 Werke aus der Sammlung sollen Positionen europäischer und amerikanischer Nachkriegskunst, darunter Vertreter der Bewegungen ZERO, Spatialismus und Light and Space, mit Arbeiten zeitgenössischer Künstler zusammenbringen. Im Mittelpunkt steht die künstlerische Auseinandersetzung mit Unendlichkeit, Licht, Raum und Wahrnehmung.

Good morning!

The Norton Simon Museum countersued the Jewish Federation Los Angeles, following the latter’s suit claiming it owned a Nazi-looted Lucas Cranach diptych in the museum collection.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art has selected artist Danh Võ for its 2027 Genesis Façade Commission.

The Biennale Jogja Foundation in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, has announced it is closing its operations after 16 years, due to political and economic turmoil.

The Headlines

CRANACH CONFUSION . The Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, California, countersued the Jewish Federation Los Angeles on Wednesday, following the latter’s suit claiming it owned a Nazi-looted Lucas Cranach diptych, Adam and Eve , made around 1530, in the museum’s collection, reports Courthouse News Service . The museum argues a previous federal lawsuit in its favor should override the Jewish Federation’s new attempt to assert ownership using a new California law allowing residents to revisit failed legal attempts to recuperate Nazi-looted art. The museum’s complaint states that “the finality of the prior von Saher judgment is beyond dispute … this court found on the merits that the museum was the sole owner of the Cranachs.”

FACING UP. The Metropolitan Museum of Art has selected artist Danh Võ for its 2027 Genesis Façade Commission , reports ArtAsiaPacific . This will be the fourth presentation installed on the museum’s 5th Avenue Beaux-Arts façade, and the Vietnamese-born artist plans to exhibit four sculptures. “A façade is the place where the museum meets the street, and it is also an expression of its values over time,” Võ said in a statement. In addition, the Norwegian Congolese artist Sandra Mujinga was chosen to make a site-specific installation for the Met’s 2027 Great Hall Commission .

The Digest

The Biennale Jogja Foundation in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, has announced it is closing its operations after 16 years of overseeing the Biennale Jogja, due to “a political regime” amid “chaotic economic and political policies, increasing censorship, and violence against activists and protesters.” [ ArtAsiaPacific ]

Three years after it was removed, plans are in the works to return a restored 1914 Confederate memorial to Arlington National Cemetery , which includes the figure of a Black woman holding the child of a white officer and a slave following his owner to war. [ NBC ]

The opening of the Centre Pompidou Paraná in southern Brazil has been delayed again amid a local government shift and is now expected to open in 2029. [ The Art Newspaper ]

Australia has returned a 14,000-year-old carved stone slab to Jordan that was found in Wadi Al Hammah and taken to the National Gallery of Australia in 1985. [ Menafn ]

Carmen Thyssen-Bornemisza , the Spanish Baroness whose family’s private collection is exhibited in the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum in Madrid, is bringing to auction a 1944 painting of a sailboat at sea by Edward Hopper on November 18 at Sotheby’s in New York, with a high estimate of $30 million. [ El Pais ]

Rubaiya Qatar , the new quadrennial on vie November 21 to April 30 in Doha, has revealed the full list of participating artists, who number over 120. [ ArtReview ]

The Kicker

DEALING WITH DISASTER . William Kentridge talks to Ocula as his latest film premieres at London’s Goodman Gallery. Titled A Nicely Built City (Never Resists Destruction) , the stop-animation film is accompanied by an exhibition of artworks. It looks at Johannesburg’s industrial transformation, and how wilderness returns to the city as its center collapses. Asked about using humor in his films, alongside the political weight of their subjects, Kentridge responded: “I don’t think there’s a contradiction between the serious and the light, and how the one illuminates the other. I think the category of the absurd is also important. Tragedy isn’t a good way of dealing with social disaster. Comedy may be closer, but the category of the absurd, which can move between the two, is central.” Read on to learn Kentridge’s thoughts on Anselm Kiefer ’s “fantastic woodcuts,” the “poetic and politically powerful” art of Alfredo Jaar , his own studio process, and more.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Craig Singer ’s horror The Block has wrapped and unveiled a first look at recent Tony award-winning actor Jack Falahee ( Death of a Salesman ) in the starring role of a writer who turns to a chilling source of inspiration.

Falahee plays Mitch James at the top of his career who becomes caught up in a murderous case of writer’s block and a fan-turned-girlfriend (Saphira Moran) obsession that becomes deadly. The movie follows the once-golden boy of horror into a mind-bending exploration of the creative process, locking the protagonist in a never-ending doom-cycle of creation and destruction.

Related Stories

Jack Falahee, Jackie Earle Haley, Chris Noth & Saphira Moran To Topline Supernatural Thriller 'The Block' From Craig Singer

Jing Ai Ng's Dark Comedy 'Forge' Adds Seven To Cast

Singer, former Creative VP at Disney, has reteamed with horror-writer Robert Dean Klein , following the success of their award-winning film 6:45 starring Michael Reed, Armin Garo and Augie Duke.

Watch on Deadline

“I’ve been developing The Block for many years,” says director and co-producer Craig Singer. “The original idea – what an artist is compelled to go through to secure their art and legacy – has always intrigued me and feels even more urgent in 2026.

“Today’s rapidly evolving, AI-driven creative landscape forces creators at every level to make artistic choices and face challenges on a scale we’ve never seen. The timing couldn’t be more relevant. The Block isn’t about jump scares; it’s a philosophic fable for our times.”

The ensemble cast of The Block also includes Thomas G. Waites ( The Thing ), Jackie Earle Haley ( Watchmen , Shutter Island ), Catherine Cocoran ( Terrifier ), Chris Noth ( Sex and the City ), Carrie Jo Crosby, Armen Garo ( Dexter: New Blood ), Michael Rodrick ( General Hospita l) and Elias Koteas ( Chicago P.D .).

The film is a co-production between Singer’s US-based production company Cascrator Films , and Australian-based production company Three777 Films which co-produced Beast starring Russell Crowe and recent slasher film The Only One starring Mel Jarnson and Moran.

The film is in post-production and does not yet have a premiere date.

article_text:
Source: Black Bear

‘Wicker’

Black Bear’s romantic comedy Wicker is the widest new release in UK and Ireland cinemas this weekend as A24’s Primetime also launches.

Opening in 676 locations, Wicker is Black Bear’s widest ever release – breaking the record set just one week before with Wildwood , which opened in 655 sites.

Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgard star in the Sundance premiere which centres on a solitary Fisherwoman who asks a Basket Weaver to make her a husband.

UK native Colman will be the biggest draw here, with her recent films The Roses , Paddington In Peru , Wonka and Wicked Little Letters having all grossed at least £10m in the territory.

Alex Hutson Fischer and Eleanor Wilson direct Wicker which also stars Peter Dinklage, Elizabeth Debicki and Richard E. Grant.

Up next is Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime which is launching in 560 sites for A24. The film grossed over £245,000 from previews in 405 cinemas on Wednesday (October 28) while it has made nearly $50m globally.

Robert Pattinson stars as the To Catch A Predator host Chris Hansen who sets out to make television history, no matter the cost. It had its world premiere in competition at the Venice Film festival and recently picked up three nominations at the Gotham Awards including best feature.

Boosters , boxing and babies

Several re-releases are taking advantage of the Halloween weekend, starting with Guillermo del Toro’s 2006 fantasy Pan’s Labyrinth in 384 venues for Studiocanal. Arrow Films has Donnie Darko in 202 venues while BFI Distribution is screening a 4K restoration of Ken Russell’s The Devils in 73 venues.

Disney opens the Venice-premiering documentary Everest: The Other Side in 200 locations, including Imax screens. The film follows two mountaineers who attempt to climb and ski down Everest’s north face. It is directed by Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi who also directed fellow thrill-seeking documentary Free Solo (£2m gross).

In event titles, Trafalgar Releasing has screenings of Manon - RBO, London 2026 as well as concert films Ozzy & Black Sabbath: Back To The Beginning and BTS World Tour ‘Arirang’ in Sao Paulo .

UK comedy Bad Day At The Office launches in 155 sites via Action Xtreme. John Hannah stars as a man who wakes up in a hotel room with a corpse and amnesia and must try to piece together the mystery. Chee Keong Cheung directs.

Source: Neon

I Love Boosters

Boots Riley’s I Love Boosters lands in 142 venues for Universal. The comedy premiered at SXSW festival and opened in the US in May with $3.8m. Featuring an ensemble cast led by Naomi Ackie and Keke Palmer, the film follows a group of female shoplifters who take aim at a fashion mogul.

Ashley Walters’ feature directing debut Animol is out in 116 locations for Sky Cinema, via Studiocanal. Set in a juvenile detention centre, the story centres on young male inmates as they navigate friendship, identity and the path to redemption. Screen Stars of Tomorrow Tut Nyuot and Sekou Diaby are among the cast which also features Stephen Graham.

Documentary Peter Asher: Everywhere Man opens in 36 cinemas via Munro Film Services. Directed by Daniel Geller and Dayna Goldfine, the film centres on the musician, producer and manager who helped foster the careers of James Taylor, Linda Ronstadt and Paul McCartney.

UK boxing biopic In The Shadows opens in 32 locations for Metis Film. Anthony Wonke’s film tells the real story of refugee Ramla Ali, who secretly pursued boxing against her parents’ wishes and went on to become the first British-Somali champion. Jasmine Jobson and Finn Cole star. The film was originally meant to be released by True Brit Entertainment before the distributor entered administration last month.

Romantic thriller City Of Masks launches in five venues for BUFF Studios. Andrea M. Catinella’s film follows a young actor who forms a bond with a ghost haunting a West End theatre.

Picturehouse Entertainment opens Hannah Bergholm’s horror Nightborn . The Berlinale premiere follows two new parents whose newborn begins to cause a rift in their relationship. Rupert Grint and Seidi Haarla star in the feature which won best film at Fantasia film festival earlier this year.

Further releases include Cannes premiere Gentle Monster via Netflix; Just Stop Oil documentary We, The Hated via Firebreak Films; and animation Arnie & Barney via Kaleidoscope.

article_text:
Keramiken, Grafiken und persönliche Dokumente aus dem Nachlass von Ivo Hauptmann und Erica von Scheel gehen nach Weimar. Was die beiden mit der Stadt verbindet

Die Klassik Stiftung Weimar erhält Keramiken, Grafiken und Dokumente aus dem Nachlass des Künstlerpaares Ivo Hauptmann und Erica von Scheel. Die Schenkung enthalte Ivo Hauptmanns Porträtstudien von Erica von Scheel und Bildnisse von Henry van de Velde in Oberägeri in der Schweiz, teilte die Stiftung mit. Das Ehepaar Hauptmann hatte van de Velde in den 1950er-Jahren in der Schweiz besucht. Eine von Erica von Scheel gebundene Ausgabe von Gerhart Hauptmann sei ebenfalls enthalten.

Der Maler Ivo Hauptmann war der älteste Sohn des Schriftstellers Gerhart Hauptmann und studierte zwischen 1904 und 1909 an der Weimarer Kunstschule. In dieser Zeit verkehrte er den Angaben zufolge im Kreis "Neues Weimar" um Harry Graf Kessler und Henry van de Velde, wo er die Keramikerin Erica von Scheel kennenlernte. Die beiden heirateten im Jahr 1912.

Keramiken aus Privatsammlung erworben

Nach eigenen Angaben erwarb die Stiftung im Verbund mit der Schenkung elf Keramiken von Erica von Scheel aus der Privatsammlung - darunter leuchtend blau glasierte Vorratsbehälter als Küchenausstattung und abstrakt ornamentierte Vasen aus Westerwälder Produktion. "Die Grafiken von Ivo Hauptmann sind ein doppelter Erfolg für Weimar: Sie sind ein Zeugnis der lebenslangen Verbundenheit des deutschen Künstlerpaars mit dem belgischen Architekten und Designer Henry van de Velde, außerdem war Ivo Hauptmann bisher nicht in den Weimarer Sammlungen vertreten", sagte Annette Ludwig, Direktorin der Museen der Klassik Stiftung Weimar.

Aus dem Nachlass wurden schriftliche Dokumente dem Goethe- und Schiller-Archiv geschenkt. Demnach sind Korrespondenzen, Manuskripte und Arbeitsunterlagen sowie handschriftliche Aufzeichnungen enthalten sowie seltene Tagebücher, historische Fotografien berühmter Künstler und Familienpapiere.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Stephen and Simon Cornwell have taken on chairmen roles at their Night Manager indie The Ink Factory amid a wave of hires and promotions.

The Cornwells, whose father was iconic British spy author John le Carré, have promoted Creative Director Michelle Wolkoff to President and Chief Creative Officer, while Ian Spence becomes Chief Financial and Operating Officer.

Simon Cornwell becomes Executive Chairman, succeeding Rod Henwood, who remains on the board and becomes Deputy Chairman. Stephen Cornwell has taken on a Creative Co-Chairman role, providing creative and strategic support across the company’s slate and operations with a primary focus on the BBC and MGM+’s The Legacy of Spies , which he is showrunning.

Related Stories

Matthew Macfadyen Is Iconic Le Carré Spy George Smiley In First Glimpse At The BBC & MGM+'s 'Legacy Of Spies'

'Ludwig' Becomes Most-Watched UK Scripted Show Of The Year

Meanwhile, and with a new season of The Night Manager soon hitting the BBC and Prime Video, The Ink Factory has hired former NBC Universal International Studios production chief Laura Burrows as production boss, re-signed Amy Basil as Chief Marketing Officer for both The Ink Factory and John le Carré Estate, and brought in Bad Wolf’s Lachlan MacKinnon as EP across the slate. Sam Costin has been promoted to a Creative Producer post in recognition of his contribution as Co-EP on the first season of Legacy of Spies .

Watch on Deadline

The Cornwells founded The Ink Factory in 2010 and have since made big hits like The Night Manager and A Most Wanted Man. Starring Matthew Macfadyen as iconic spymaster George Smiley, Legacy of Spies is anticipated to be the next big one.

Simon and Stephen Cornwell said: “Over sixteen years and counting, we have been custodians of both our father’s legacy through the adaptations The Ink Factory has made, as well as realising an array of work from the most compelling storytellers and filmmakers working today. We’re exhilarated by the possibilities that lie ahead and the opportunities for Michele and Ian – vital members of the Ink Factory family for many years now – to work alongside us as we continue to guide the direction of our future and broaden our scope and slate. We are also delighted to welcome Laura and Lachlan, and the returning Amy, to the team as we enter the next era of Ink.”

Wolkoff described her new role as a “unique privilege,” coming “at such an important moment for Ink Factory and to help shape the company’s next chapter.” “What John le Carré built is a world of ideas, attitudes, incredible characters, and tradecraft – through stories which artfully balance being both thrilling entertainment and a deep interrogation of the important questions of our time,” she added. “I am excited to continue exploring that world, in ways that expand what we understand adaptation to be.”

article_text:
東京都写真美術館のB1F展示室では、12月1日より岡田敦の写真展「幻の馬 Yururi Island 1950-2026」が始まる。

本展では、2011年から岡田敦が撮影してきたユルリ島の馬の写真が展示される。ユルリ島は、根室半島・昆布盛漁業港の南東2kmの沖合に位置する現代の“ロスト・ワールド”である。この言葉はコナン・ドイルが著した、断崖に囲まれた人跡未踏の台地に絶滅したはずの動物たちの王国があったという空想小説のタイトルだが、ユルリ島という無人島もまた、立ち入りが制限されて人は近づけない。そしてここには人知れず馬たちが、それも雌馬だけが暮らしている。岡田はそんなロスト・ワールドの目撃者として存在している。雌馬だけとなった群れは誕生の可能性を持たず、1950年に島に移入された馬の子孫は岡田が撮影を始めた2011年には10数頭、そして今は2頭にまで減った。

この展覧会で見られる写真に刻印されているのは、いわば蝋燭の炎が消えんとする瞬間の揺めきだ。その儚くも美しい命の証の光が人々の記憶にどのように残っていくのか、その目で確かめたい。

Films and events

Shorts

As the Years Roll By

In reflecting on the past or embracing unexpected futures, time flows through people’s connection with others and the earth, in these shorts on life in the later years.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Total running time 97min

Programmed by Sky Lewis, Victoria Millington

Content advice This short film programme contains scenes of graphic violence or injury.

Agnes

Director-screenwriter Leah Vlemmiks

UK-Canada 2026. 11min

Under pressure from her adult daughter to move and become a live-in babysitter, Agnes finds agency in an unexpected place.

Listen

Director Taliesin Black-Brown

USA 2026. 15min

As his mother slips away as a result of dementia, an Alaskan sound recordist listens for what remains.

Geronto

Director Mark Pluck

Screenwriter Christopher Sherwood

UK 2026. 18min

Late one night, Younger, a man in his 20s, meets Older, a man in his 60s, at a discreet London pub.

All Change

Director-screenwriter Lena Molander

UK 2025. 3min

While talking on a train journey, two men admit to regrets over their friendship.

In the Morning Sun

Director-screenwriter Serville Poblete

Philippines-Canada 2026. 21min

A gentle portrait of aging, migration and memory, inspired by the filmmaker’s desire to preserve the warmth of his parents.

A Grief Encounter

Director-screenwriter James Ashley McLaren

Australia 2026. 12min

A struggling taxidermy artist’s flirtation with a customer takes an interesting turn.

Untitled Woman

Director Camille Summers-Valli

Screenwriters Rosemarie Vind, Camille Summers-Valli

UK 2026. 17min

Dawn is invisible to those around her in a world that favours youth, until she fights back.

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

I See Myself

From silent protests and secret ponderings to vocal uprisings and drastic acts, watch people endeavour to carve a bigger space for themselves in a world that’s trying to box them in.

Altered States

Fractured memories and uncertain fates are examined in shorts featuring our unshakeable resolve.

Life / Drawing

A selection of animated shorts exploring what connects us to people, the world around us and, most importantly, ourselves.

article_text:
Christie’s first fine art auction in Abu Dhabi concluded the sale reaching a total of USD 8,940,800. Entitled MAWASIM: 20 Years of Modern and Contemporary Middle Eastern Art the auction celebrated twenty years since Christie’s hosted its first sale in the UAE led by auctioneer Yü-Ge Wang.

Leading the results was Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian’s Variations on the Hexagon (2006), which realised USD 844,800, with bidding extending to nearly seven minutes, and reached more than its pre-sale estimate of USD 150,000–250,000. Fahrelnissa Zeid’s Composition (1948–1949) followed at USD 524,800, while Ali Banisadr’s Homo Deus (2018) achieved USD 512,000. Paul Guiragossian’s Noces (Wedding) , Mahmoud Saïd’s Portrait de Princesse Fadia (1952) and Fahrelnissa Zeid’s Endless Thoughts (1970s) each realised USD 486,400. Further results included Samia Halaby’s Yesterday (1978), which achieved USD 358,400, Ayman Baalbaki’s Babel Tower (2012), which realised USD 281,600, and Farhad Moshiri’s Untitled (2003), which sold for USD 230,400.

Last night, the auction also set nine new records, including world auction records for Faisel Laibi Sahi’s Baghdad Café (The Coffee Shop) (2016 ) that went for USD 512,000, Jellal Ben Abdallah’s (The Female Musicians) (1973) at USD 204,800 and Juliana Seraphim’s Femme Fleur (Flower Woman) (1973) at USD 83,200. Guiragossian’s Noces (Wedding) (1958–59) and Halaby’s Three Way Seven (1982), set the auction record for their mediums.

Nabil Kanso ’s Mother and Child (Kuwait/Desert Storm series) (1991), alongside works by Emirati artists Rami Farook’s Oh God, I Ask You for Peace of Mind (2024), Fatma Lootah’s Untitled (2011) and Afra Al Dhaheri ’s No. 22 (Spaces for Improvisation series) (2022), which saw all four artists make their auction debuts.

The auction also featured works from prominent regional collections, including the Dalloul Collection in Beirut, which presented a selection of works including artists such as Ben Abdallah, whose Les Misiciennes (The Female Musicians) (1973) sold for USD 204,800, Laibi Sahi’s Baghdad Café (The Coffee Shop) (2016) achieved USD 512,000 and Halaby, whose Tashkeel I (2013) realised USD 204,800. The Barjeel Art Foundation in Sharjah also presented works from its collection, including Jumana El Husseini’s Al Qods (Jerusalem) (1975), which achieved USD 76,800, Nadia Saïkali’s Mandala Bleu Nuit (Midnight Blue Mandala) (1982), which sold for USD 40,960 and Seta Manoukian’s Figures (1967), which realised USD 23,040, among others.

Addressing the significance of the auction for Christie’s presence in the region, Anthea Peers, president of Christie’s EMEA, noted, “What an exceptional week. Two decades on from our first auction in the UAE, it’s thrilling to have held the first fine art auction in Abu Dhabi. We welcomed so many collectors together with those passionate about art and artists from the wider region to our view, programming and events. The response to MAWASIM has been hugely rewarding. It is a wonderful milestone in Christie’s history in the UAE, and we look forward to all that comes next.”

Dr Ridha Moumni, Chairman, Middle East and Africa, Christie’s, and Marie-Claire Thijsen , Head of Sale and Specialist, Christie’s UK and UAE, both noted in a joint statement: “Tonight’s results highlight the compelling selection of modern and contemporary art from the Middle East and North Africa offered in MAWASIM , reflecting the diversity of artistic languages, geographies and generations that have emerged across the region. We were delighted to see that more than 30 percent of registrants were Millennial and Gen Z, and in addition 37 percent were new to Christie’s this evening. The breadth of bidding across the sale demonstrates the international interest this category has achieved today. Its scale reflects the depth of the region’s art sector and its capacity to support a major sale of this kind.”

article_text:
2026 has already been a wild year for horror, from low-budget box office hits (“Backrooms,” “Obsession”) to sequels the world could have lived without (“Scream 7,” “The Strangers – Chapter 3”). In a year loaded with scary movies, many of them were good-to-great, a welcome surprise that kept multiplexes busy. Below are the year’s standouts, including some honorable mentions also worth watching.

There were also several exciting genre movies released this year — such as Adam Wingard’s “Onslaught,” Na Hong-jin’s “Hope” and David Robert Mitchell’s “The End of Oak Street” — that flirted with being horror, but ultimately seemed to fit better in categories like action, sci-fi and adventure.

Note: Only films that were fully released in 2026 so far were up for inclusion, so no festival favorites or titles that haven’t hit theaters yet — like Zachary Wigon’s “Victorian Psycho” or Robert Eggers’ “Werwulf”— could make the cut.

Honorable Mentions:

Send Help (20th Century Studios) — Sam Raimi’s return to horror was this stylish little survival thriller, with great performances from Rachel McAdams and Dylan O’Brien as two at-odds office workers who are trying to get off a deserted island after a gnarly plane crash. While the overarching plot is a little predictable, there are some great twists and turns along the way.

Buffet Infinity (Yellow Veil Pictures) — This wild feature made up entirely of fake commercials is a trip to watch, and will delight any fans “Tim and Eric Awesome Show, Great Job!” or other lost media madness. Although the clips feel disconnected at first, it’s soon clear that a local sinkhole might be behind a restaurant war, a religious cult and plenty more unpredictable twists and turns. It’s not for everybody, but those who can get on the same wavelength as “Buffet Infinity” will be richly rewarded.

Saccharine (Independent Film Company and Shudder) — Natalie Erika James’ timely film considers the dark side of fad diets, as a med student (Midori Francis) realizes that ingesting the ashes of the dead is the best miracle drug around. While it’s not the white-knuckle ride many fans might want, it’s an effectively gross body horror story that has plenty to say.

Backrooms Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection A24 Kane Parsons’ dizzyingly accomplished film is a masterwork in tone and tension, dropping Chiwetel Ejiofor and Renate Reinsve into an endless maze of liminal spaces that are claustrophobic, confusing and overwhelming. It’s hard to describe why “Backrooms” works to the unconverted or unconvinced, but the incredible production design and camerawork of Jeremy Cox make up for any limitations of the sketch of a script. It’s exciting to see what Parsons will do with a next chapter — and maybe even what he could do beyond the limitations of his own space.

Exit 8 Image Credit: Courtesy of Toho, Cannes Film Festival Neon Genki Kawamura’s video game adaptation concerns a man (Kazunari Ninomiya) who cannot escape walking a long section of a subway hallway, stuck in an endless repetition. Yet he’s soon able to discern tiny clues about how to move forward and pass through some dark reverberations of his life and decisions to get to the other side. While the hook grows a little thin, it’s by necessity, as the audience begins to feel as stuck and hopeless as its main character, and each new detail pointing to escape is a breath of fresh air.

Mārama Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection Dark Sky Films and Watermelon Pictures Taratoa Stappard’s gothic tale examines Māori culture and the colonizers who almost snuffed it out. Ariāna Osborne is spellbinding as the title character, a Victorian-era woman who travels to England to find out more about her lineage, only to become a governess for a mysterious man with an affinity for her Māori heritage. As things get dark, Stappard’s vision grows even more lush, with an atmosphere teeming with evil.

Faces of Death Image Credit: Courtesy of Independent Film Company and Shudder Independent Film Company The idea of releasing a new “Faces of Death” may have once seemed inconceivable, but the creative partnership of Isa Mazzei and Daniel Goldhaber was able to spin the seminal oddity into a tight serial killer movie with a deeper motive. Dacre Montgomery plays a maniac obsessed with the original film, which was purported to include real-life depictions of violence. His recreation of the goriest bits nabs the attention of a content moderator (Barbie Ferreira) and a bloody game of cat and mouse begins. Mazzei and Goldhaber have plenty of keen observations on influencer and online culture, while Montgomery is genuinely chilling as a killer who does his best to blend in and be forgettable.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple Image Credit: ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Sony Pictures Releasing A heady, heartfelt spin on zombie movies, Nia DaCosta helms this fourth chapter in the series, which dodges nearly every expectation. Ralph Fiennes stars as Dr. Ian Kelson, who lives alone in the post-breakout world, coming closer and closer to finding a cure with the help of his undead friend, Samson (Chi Lewis-Parry). Unfortunately, as the pair develops a partnership, a roving leader of violent kids, Sir Lord Jimmy Crystal (Jack O’Connell), roams the countryside looking for people to antagonize. Many thought-provoking moments — as well as one wild Iron Maiden dance sequence — follow in Alex Garland’s sharp script, which begs for another installment.

Leviticus Image Credit: Courtesy of Neon Neon A touching love story about two boys in Australia becomes a nightmare when a religious conversion therapy turns the person they love the most into the thing trying to kill them. From there, Naim (Joe Bird) and Ryan (Stacy Clausen) are unsure if the object of their affection is real or a beast out for blood. Building a heartfelt and tender romance, “Leviticus” traffics more in tension than flat-out scares, but it’s unlikely there will be a more affecting horror movie this year.

They Will Kill You Image Credit: Courtesy of Warner Bros. Pictures Warner Bros. Pictures Zazie Beetz kicks an enormous amount of ass as brutal fighter Asia Reaves in this horror-action-comedy. When she infiltrates a hotel that she believes has kidnapped her maid sister, Asia must brawl her way through endless villains loyal to the satanic cult, who are invincible but can get mutilated along the way, leading to surreal scenes like the adventures of a dislodged, crawling eyeball. An early “Kill Bill”-esque showdown and a torch-lit beatdown in a ballroom are among the flashy setpieces. Beetz is a pro at the stunt choreography, showing the toil of inflicting and receiving extreme pain. Cinematographer Isaac Bauman also shoots her in inspired ways, touching on pop touchstones like comic books and martial arts films.

Appofeniacs Image Credit: Magenta Edge Films Magenta Edge Films An internet troll with an axe to grind sets off this interwoven tale of mayhem from first-time feature director Chris Marrs Piliero. This microbudget thriller stretches out every dollar for a visually inventive look at how deepfakes can disrupt the lives of people even after they log off. Filled with shocking twists and some great practical effects, it’s a film as funny and squirm-inducing as it is prescient.

Her Private Hell Image Credit: Neon Neon Nicolas Winding Refn’s received a flurry of mixed-to-negative reviews, but ignore them. No one is making films like Refn, and if you can get on his wavelength, it’s a hell of a ride worth taking. Sophie Thatcher, Charles Melton and Havana Rose Liu are hypnotic in this giallo-influenced head trip. Endlessly stylish and bold, “Her Private Hell” is destined for cult classic status.

Resident Evil Image Credit: ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Sony Pictures Releasing Third time’s a charm, as Zach Cregger cements his winning run as a horror auteur with this roller coaster ride of a video game adaptation. Austin Abrams is a perfect audience surrogate, injecting humor into the increasingly outrageous situations as his life quickly becomes a zombie-fueled chase. It’s a completely different vibe from both “Barbarian” and “Weapons,” and it’s so exciting to think about what Cregger has up his sleeve next.

Touch Me Image Credit: Dustin Supencheck Yellow Veil Pictures Addison Heimann’s wild take on an alien creature feature blends up countless inspirations: tentacle sex, drugs, Japanese cinema, ‘80s hip-hop dance and throuples, to name a few. Yet it’s a kaleidoscopic adventure: A slacker (Olivia Taylor Dudley) and her gay best friend (Jordan Gavaris) both start hooking up with an extraterrestrial (Lou Taylor Pucci) whose powers make them feel like they’re in a drug-fueled euphoria. Unfortunately, the alien has a darker plan than he lets on, and our unlikely heroes must save humanity. With plenty of humor and unpredictable moments, it’s a joy to take a ride in Heimann’s mind.

Hokum Image Credit: Courtesy of Neon Neon An old-school haunted house bonanza, Damian McCarthy’s latest drops Ohm (Adam Scott) into an Irish hotel that’s filled with secrets. When he gets locked in, he has to solve a murder mystery before he’s overtaken by scores of supernatural happenings. The set design is remarkable, toeing the line between coziness and mustiness that makes the hotel come alive for all of the senses. Scott is a remarkable lead, as he’s playing Ohm as such an asshole, but his journey of self-awareness soon becomes as engaging as what happened to the dead body. It’s all threaded by some highbrow jump scares that make for a great rollercoaster ride, best enjoyed at a crowded multiplex.

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma Image Credit: Courtesy of MUBI Mubi Jane Schoenbrun’s winning rom-com is rooted in an obsessive love for slashers, and begs for repeat viewings to luxuriate in all of the pop culture nods embedded within. But the film is not merely a pastiche: Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson have crackling chemistry together, and the film is filled with indelible imagery and memorable scenes, from a sexually charged KFC dinner to a spirited massacre scene soundtracked to Counting Crows.

Obsession Image Credit: ©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection Focus Features Before all of the thinkpieces and analysis, “Obsession” started life as a nasty little thriller that mixed an old-school monkey’s paw scenario with a contemporary look at life in the friendzone. It’s a simple story, but twisty scares and an all-timer performance from Inde Navarrette made the fear burrow deep into audiences’ minds. Countless WTF moments have been debated for months, and that bleak ending ensured the film stayed unforgettable long after leaving the theater.
